findings.paper_title: 01 final Council tax and General Fund report 2026-27 COUNCIL
findings.headline: Capital strategy remains significantly underfunded despite new £1.2m annual revenue contribution, with unfunded bids totalling £1.6m over MTFS.
findings.detail: The council has restricted capital investment to fix-on-fail for years due to resource constraints. A new stock condition survey for 2026/27 is expected to identify further required works to community, operational and leisure buildings, but capital bids still exceed available resources. Over 2026/27-2029/30 there are £1.6m in growth bids not funded.
findings.matters: Lenders assess councils' ability to maintain asset bases and service infrastructure. Persistent capital underfunding and deferred maintenance create future liabilities and may signal deteriorating condition of council-held assets used in service delivery.
findings.quote: However, Members should note that even with the additional resources set out above there are still a number of capital bids not funded and the stock condition survey included in the proposed 2026/27 programme may identify further works required to the Council's community, operational and leisure buildings once completed.

findings.paper_title: 01 final Council tax and General Fund report 2026-27 COUNCIL
findings.headline: Business rates reset eliminates £1.2m annual gains previously realised, with tariff payment rising from £19.49m to £22.79m.
findings.detail: In 2025/26 the council retained £1.2m in business rates gains above baseline. The Fair Funding reform for 2026/27 includes a complete reset of business rates with increased tariff payments to government. This removes a material revenue stream: the council now projects zero gains for 2026/27-2029/30, forcing greater reliance on fixed funding settlements and council tax.
findings.matters: Lenders depend on stable revenue sources; loss of a £1.2m annual income line materially changes the council's resilience. The shift from tariff of £19.49m to £22.79m represents net redistribution to government that squeezes retained business rates and reduces financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Business rates retained 2025/26: £1.2m gains; 2026/27 onwards: £0m gains projected. Tariff payment: £19.49m (2025/26) → £22.79m (2026/27), an increase of £3.30m.
findings.quote: with the complete reset of business rates for 2026/27 and a projected reduction in gains against the 2025/26 estimate (see paragraph 4.4.7) no gains are currently included for the period 2026/27-2029/30.

findings.paper_title: 3a Appendix D Section 25 Statement by the CFO
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation transition costs uncertain due to government's undecided final structure
findings.detail: The council has set aside £560K for 2026/27 and £500K for 2027/28 for LGR transition costs, with a recommended contingency of an additional £500K. However, the government has not yet decided the final structure of the new unitary authority, creating material uncertainty about whether these provisions will prove adequate.
findings.matters: Unbudgeted transition costs could force drawdown of reserves or service cuts during a period when the council is already dealing with ongoing structural deficits and LGR uncertainty itself affects future financial viability and council management bandwidth.
findings.figures: £560K (2026/27), £500K (2027/28), plus recommended £500K contingency; final LGR structure not yet decided

findings.paper_title: 3a Appendix D Section 25 Statement by the CFO
findings.headline: HRA earmarked debt reserve drawn down from £16.7M to £8.7M in one year
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account's earmarked reserve specifically held for debt repayment is forecast to fall from £16.7M as at 1 April 2026 to £8.7M as at 1 April 2027. This represents a 48% reduction in HRA's dedicated debt management reserve in a single year.
findings.matters: A steep drawdown of reserves designated for debt management reduces the council's flexibility to respond to interest rate movements, refinancing risks, or unexpected housing maintenance costs, particularly significant given the scale of HRA borrowing (£35.61M planned for 2026/27).
findings.figures: HRA earmarked debt reserve: £16.7M (1 April 2026) → £8.7M (1 April 2027)
findings.quote: The HRA also has an earmarked reserve for the repayment of debt which is estimated to be £16.7Million as at 1st April 2026 and £8.7Million as at 1 April 2027.

findings.paper_title: 3a Appendix D Section 25 Statement by the CFO
findings.headline: £45.11M external borrowing planned for 2026/27, including £7.789M conversion of internal debt to external
findings.detail: The council plans to borrow £45.11M in 2026/27: £35.61M for HRA capital, £7.789M to convert internal debt arrangements to external borrowing, and £9.5M for General Fund (with £5.9M short-term). The conversion of internal arrangements to external debt increases the council's formal external liability and debt servicing obligations.
findings.matters: A material increase in external borrowing for a council entering LGR transition increases leverage during a period of structural uncertainty. The debt conversion is particularly significant as it formalises existing obligations as external debt.
findings.figures: £45.11M total borrowing: £35.61M HRA capital, £7.789M internal debt conversion, £9.5M General Fund
findings.quote: the Council has a need to borrow in 2026/27 £45.11Million including for the HRA £35.61Million for capital plus £7.789Million for conversion of internal debt to borrowing and £9.5Million for the General Fund of which £5.9Million is short term borrowing

findings.headline: £800K in new savings still unidentified for 2027/28-2029/30
findings.detail: The CFO has identified that additional BTB savings options are required for 2027/28-2029/30 of £800K to maintain a balanced General Fund budget. The council has proposed these could be met from annual fees and charges increases, but this represents a gap in the forward financial plan that has not yet been solved.
findings.matters: An outstanding savings requirement this far out suggests either service cuts or fee rises are ahead, and demonstrates the council's ongoing structural deficit after the current year's settlement.
findings.figures: £800K savings requirement for 2027/28-2029/30
findings.quote: The CFO has identified that further new BTB savings options are required for 2027/28-2029/30 of just £800K to ensure a balanced General Fund budget which could be met from annual fees and charges increases.

findings.headline: Rising debt burden with HRA affordability risk flagged
findings.detail: Total external debt forecast to reach £345.6M by 2028/29. HRA financing costs as ratio of net revenue stream forecast at 15% (2026/27) and 16% (2027/28), significantly above the General Fund ratio of 8%. This reflects high HRA debt burden from self-financing.
findings.matters: HRA is carrying disproportionate debt burden relative to its income stream, creating affordability risk if rents cannot rise in line with rates or if service demands change.

findings.headline: General Fund reserves declining 36% over single financial year
findings.detail: General Fund reserves (including earmarked) forecast to fall from £105.2M (2025/26) to £66.8M (2026/27), a decline of £38.4M or 36%. While they recover modestly to £74.1M by 2028/29, this represents a significant erosion of financial resilience in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Rapid reserve depletion reduces the council's buffer to absorb service pressures or revenue shortfalls, increasing financial fragility.
findings.quote: Year End Resources show Fund balances / reserves declining from £105,165k (2025/26 Estimate) to £66,777k (2026/27 Estimate)

findings.headline: Interest rate risk: under-borrowing strategy viability dependent on rate differentials
findings.detail: Council explicitly states that its strategy of minimising external borrowing 'only remains financially viable while cash balances are high and the differentials between investment income and borrowing rates remain.' If conditions change, the council may need to borrow at higher rates increasing revenue costs.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's financial position is dependent on interest rate arbitrage that may not persist, creating potential budget pressure.
findings.figures: Current investment earnings forecast 3.5% (2026/27), BOE base rate 3.75% expected to fall to 3.25% by March 2027
findings.quote: The current policy of minimising external borrowing only remains financially viable while cash balances are high and the differentials between investment income and borrowing rates remain. As these conditions change the Council may need to take borrowing at higher rates which would increase revenue costs.

findings.headline: HRA carrying £246M of PWLB debt with 30+ year repayment horizon
findings.detail: Housing Revenue Account has externally borrowed £246.2M from PWLB, dominated by £194.9M self-financing payment made to central government in 2012. Forecast repayment date is 2055/56 including periods of refinancing. Council has heightened reserves provision to mitigate risks of higher borrowed business plan.
findings.matters: HRA debt burden is structural and very long-dated. The council recognises risk through elevated reserves, suggesting concerns about affordability if rates remain elevated.
findings.figures: HRA external PWLB borrowing £246.231M; target average borrowing rate 4.8% (2025/26 and 2026/27); forecast repayment 2055/56
findings.quote: It is currently forecast that the HRA outstanding debt will be repaid in full by 2055/56, including period of re-financing.

findings.headline: Inflationary pressures forcing capital programme under active review
findings.detail: The council is monitoring and reviewing remaining planned borrowing in the capital programme because of inflationary pressures, shortages of materials and labour. This adds uncertainty to costs and may trigger mid-year changes.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know that capital costs are uncertain and may require additional funding beyond current forecasts.
findings.figures: £12M PWLB borrowing agreed to be remitted 26 January 2026 for HRA refinancing
findings.quote: Remaining planned borrowing in the capital programme is being kept under regular review because of inflationary pressures, shortages of materials and labour.

findings.headline: Capital expenditure rising 73% in 2026/27 with £45.1M funded by new borrowing
findings.detail: Total capital expenditure forecast at £122.2M for 2026/27 compared to £70.4M in 2025/26. Of this, £45.1M requires new borrowing (compared to £20.6M in 2025/26). This is the largest borrowing-funded capital programme in the forecast period.
findings.matters: A sharp increase in capital borrowing requirement signals major infrastructure or regeneration commitments that will consume the council's debt capacity.

findings.quote: Members are asked to approve the capital expenditure forecasts: Non-HRA £46,551k, HRA £75,634k, Total £122,185k

findings.headline: Cash reserves forecast to fall from £56m to £30m by 2026/27 as capital programme accelerates
findings.detail: Cash reserves fell from £56M to £42M in just three months (31 Dec 2025 to forecast 31 March 2026), a 25% decline. By 2026/27 reserves are forecast to fall further to £30M. This rapid depletion is being driven by a capital programme that more than doubled in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Depleting cash reserves reduce financial flexibility and liquidity cushion, forcing reliance on external borrowing at potentially higher rates.
findings.figures: £56M (31 Dec 2025) → £42M (31 March 2026 forecast) → £30M (2026/27 forecast)
findings.quote: Cash balances as of 31 December 2025 were £56Million and are forecast to be £42Million as of 31 March 2026.

findings.headline: Significant shift from cash-funded to external borrowing in medium term
findings.detail: The council is moving away from using cash reserves to fund capital expenditure and will need to externally borrow. Currently under-borrowed with £215M net treasury borrowing at end 2025, but investment balances are already allocated and unavailable for debt repayment. This forces a funding shift.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that the council's borrowing requirement is structural and growing, not cyclical, and that cash reserves cannot offset it.
findings.figures: External debt forecast at £298.8M (2025/26) rising to £333.874M (2026/27); net treasury borrowing £215M at 31 December 2025
findings.quote: Investment balances held by the Council are already allocated and are not available for repayment of debt or additional capital expenditure. As a result, the Council will need to externally borrow to replace internal borrowing in the medium term.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Stevenage Borough Council- Audit Completion Report 2024-25 - FINAL
findings.headline: Auditor intends to disclaim opinion on 2024/25 financial statements
findings.detail: The auditors cannot form an opinion on the 2024/25 accounts due to insufficient assurance over opening balances from three consecutive prior-year disclaimed opinions (2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24). Time constraints imposed by the statutory backstop of 27 February 2026 mean necessary audit procedures cannot be completed. findings.headline: The council will reclaim £1,057,660.39 in historically overpaid Minimum Revenue Provision across 2025/26 and subsequent years
findings.detail: Following a 2019/20 review of asset useful lives, the council discovered it had overpaid its MRP (the mandatory annual charge to revenue for debt repayment). This overpayment means no MRP charge is required for regeneration assets until 2025/26, when £89,144.79 will be charged, with the remaining balance utilised in later years.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand the council's actual revenue requirements for debt servicing. A material adjustment to historic MRP affects the council's reported budget position and available resources, and may indicate previous over-conservatism in debt accounting.
findings.figures: £1,057,660.39 total overpayment; £89,144.79 partial charge in 2025/26; asset lives now range from 7 years (ICT equipment) to 50 years (investment properties and carparks)
findings.quote: The overpayment of £1,057,660.39 resulted in no MRP needing to be charged to the accounts for the regeneration assets until 2025/26, when a partial charge will be applied, utilising the remainder of the overpayment balance.

findings.headline: Staffing is largely protected; only one occupied post affected across all savings
findings.detail: Two staffing proposals: S4 deletes a vacant Regeneration post (£46,780); S7 deletes one Customer Services management role with no redundancy expected, managed through existing temporary arrangements (£12,150). No other post reductions proposed. Total occupied-post reduction: one management role.
findings.matters: A council achieving savings without significant redundancy suggests either overstaffing in specific areas or that staffing is protected as a policy priority, limiting further headroom for future cost control.
findings.figures: One management post deletion (£12,150); one vacant post deletion (£46,780); total £58,930 of £84,640 (70% of all savings)
findings.quote: A management saving is proposed within the Customer Service Centre through the deletion of one management role. No redundancies are expected, as temporary arrangements are currently in place.

findings.headline: ICT M365 migration is conditional on proof of concept and delivers no year 1 benefit
findings.detail: S5 budgets £1,628,850 for ICT but proposes no year 1 saving. The proposal states 'Depending on the outcome of a proof of the concepts over the next nine months, replacing the virtual desktop solution with M365 will result in further savings of £40k in 2028/29.' No committed saving in this or the next budget cycle.
findings.matters: A material budget area (£1.6m) shows no planned efficiency gain and any benefit is speculative and two years away, suggesting either current systems are not fit for change or savings are not yet quantified.
findings.figures: £1,628,850 current ICT budget; £0 year 1 saving; £40k conditional in 2028/29
findings.quote: Depending on the outcome of a proof of the concepts over the next nine months, replacing the virtual desktop solution with M365 will result in further savings of £40k in 2028/29.

findings.headline: Material income streams deferred: bin charges for new developments not materialising until 2027/28
findings.detail: S9 proposes charging developers for waste and recycling receptacles, projecting £8,100 in year 2 income. The paper states approval is sought now to allow implementation from 2025/26, but 'the projected additional income from bin deliveries will not materialise until 2027/28 onwards'. This creates a timing gap between approval and cash benefit.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know when income actually arrives; a deferred income stream is weaker than one materialising in the current budget year.
findings.figures: £8,100 year 2, but no year 1 impact; implementation approval sought but income only from 2027/28
findings.quote: Although the projected additional income from bin deliveries will not materialise until 2027/28 onwards, approval is sought at this stage to enable officers to begin issuing charging packs to external developers from this financial year (2025/26).

findings.headline: Budget balanced almost entirely through income generation and fee increases rather than cost cuts
findings.detail: Of ten proposals, only two reduce actual spending (delete one vacant post, one management role). The rest are new or increased fees: planning charges (£10,910), banner advertising (£4,000), bin charges for developers (£8,100), and waste service charges (£5,800). The ICT savings are conditional and future-dated.
findings.matters: A budget balanced through charges rather than expenditure control suggests revenue pressure and may affect residents' and developers' willingness to engage with the council.
findings.figures: £84,640 year 1 total; £46,780 from one post deletion, £12,150 from one management role deletion; remaining £25,710 from fees and new charges
findings.quote: Introduction of FastTrack applications... A typical FastTrack application fee charge will be £194 additional and for FastTrack certificate will be £97 additional. Uplift in pre-application fees across a range of application types.

findings.headline: Council reclaiming £1.06m MRP overpayment identified in 2019/20 asset-life review
findings.detail: Following an asset useful-life review in 2019/20, the council identified overpaid MRP of £1,057,660.39. This amount is being reclaimed in annual tranches 2020/21–2025/26, which eliminates or reduces MRP charges for regeneration assets during those years.
findings.matters: Material accounting adjustment affecting recorded debt position and annual budget headroom; shows careful MRP management but also defers recognised debt repayment costs
findings.quote: The overpayment of £1,057,660.39 result ed in no MRP needing to be charged to the accounts for the regeneration assets until 2025/26, when a partial charge will be applied, utilising the remainder of the overpayment balance.

findings.headline: Council capital programme has been unfunded since 2013/14, financed through investment balances rather than external borrowing
findings.detail: For 13 years, Stevenage has not received sufficient capital funding to fully fund its capital programme and has relied on using investment balances to finance capital expenditure. This is not presented as a current crisis but reflects a structural funding model.
findings.matters: Shows reliance on reserves for capital investment; relevant to assess reserve depletion trajectory and future capital spending capacity
findings.figures: From 2013/14 (13 years unfunded)
findings.quote: From 2013/14, the council has not had a fully funded capital programme, and although there has not been a need to borrow in full externally, due to the use of investment balances, it is necessary to make adequate provision for the repayment of debt in the form of Minimum Revenue Provision.

findings.headline: Net zero decarbonisation by 2050 unaffordable at £110-128M; not included in 30-year plan
findings.detail: Council is committed to net zero by 2050 but has explicitly excluded full decarbonisation from the HRA Business Plan as 'unaffordable without significant external funding.' The plan covers EPC C compliance by 2030 (funded) but leaves £110-128M of net zero retrofit costs unfunded. This is a known long-term liability and source of future budget pressure.
findings.matters: A £110-128M unfunded long-term commitment represents future financial risk. Tightening of energy standards or higher retrofit costs could force material reallocation of capital priorities.
findings.figures: £110M–£128M estimated unaffordable cost for net zero by 2050; 2,200 homes still require investment for EPC C standard
findings.quote: full decarbonisation to achieve net zero by 2050 is not included in the current plan due to the estimated additional cost of £110m –£128m, which is unaffordable without significant external funding.

findings.headline: Government rent policy remains unconfirmed, creating £209K income risk on rent convergence delayed until January 2026
findings.detail: Budget excludes £209K from rent convergence policy not yet confirmed by Government. The paper states 'the Government have delayed the announcement on rent convergence until January 2026.' While the HRA Business Plan assumes convergence at £1 per week cap, the final budget deliberately removes this income pending policy confirmation, creating contingent income dependent on external Government decision.
findings.matters: Income planning depends on unconfirmed external policy. This creates planning uncertainty and makes cash forecasts dependent on Government action outside council control.
findings.figures: £209K conditional income from rent convergence; average increase of £1 per week if implemented; affects 6,703 social rent properties
findings.quote: As the Government has not confirmed whether they will include rent convergence in the final rent standard for April 2026, the final budget proposal excludes the impact of this

findings.headline: One-off Right to Buy windfall of £21M masks structural capital funding gap that re-emerges after 2027/28
findings.detail: Temporary spike in RTB sales from 8 per annum to 100+ in 2025/26 and ~20 in 2026/27 generates one-off capital receipt of £21M. However, 'after this the lower discount and further changes to the scheme are likely to reduce future disposals, (estimated to be 8 RTB's per annum from 2027/28).' This means capital receipts drop dramatically after 2027. The capital programme relies on this windfall; once it ends, a structural funding gap emerges.
findings.matters: Temporary windfall obscures structural underfunding of capital programmes. Once receipts normalize, the council faces either material capital cuts, further borrowing, or alternative funding arrangements.
findings.figures: One-off capital receipt £21M from RTB sales; current sales 100+ per annum; normalized to 8 per annum from 2027/28; five-year capital programme £240M
findings.quote: It is also anticipated that there will be a further 20 sales in 2026/27, but after this the lower discount and further changes to the scheme are likely to reduce future disposals, (estimated to be 8 RTB's per annum from 2027/28).

findings.headline: HRA minimum reserves increased £3.7M to £10M due to elevated operational and financial risks
findings.detail: Minimum balance requirement increased from £6.3M to £10M. Council explicitly states this reflects 'the change in operational risks identified in the latest business plan projections' including 'larger investment needs, large savings targets in the medium term and higher borrowing levels, with uncertainty on future interest rates.' Projected 2026/27 HRA balance of £10.094M leaves only £94K headroom above the new minimum.
findings.matters: Reserve increase signals deteriorated risk profile in the council's own assessment. Tighter headroom above minimum reduces financial flexibility and indicates stress in the underlying position.
findings.figures: Minimum balances increased from £6.3M to £10M; projected year-end balance £10.094M (£94K above minimum)
findings.quote: Current minimum balances have increased from last year (£6.3Million to £10Million) to reflect the change in operational risks identified in the latest business plan projections.

findings.headline: Peak HRA debt of £354M in year 6 depends on interest rate assumptions; £92M refinancing due 2029/30 at uncertain future rates
findings.detail: Debt peaks at £354M by 2031/32. Current plan assumes 4.8% average interest rates for next two years, declining to 3.75% long-term. However, the council notes 'Current interest rates on Government debt remain higher than the much lower levels seen in the past decade.' A material refinancing of £92M is planned for 2029/30 at uncertain timing and rates. Interest costs estimated at £9.7M for 2026/27.
findings.matters: Interest rate assumptions underpinning debt affordability may not hold. If rates remain elevated, debt serviceability and the viability of the capital programme are at risk. The 2029/30 refinancing is a material refinancing event.
findings.figures: Peak debt £354M (2031/32); new borrowing £43.4M (2026/27); interest payable £9.7M (2026/27); assumed rate 4.8% (near-term) declining to 3.75% (long-term); £92M refinancing in 2029/30
findings.quote: Current interest rates on Government debt remain higher than the much lower levels seen in the past decade and this has led to a revised debt strategy in the HRA Business Plan.

findings.headline: Regulator gave C2 consumer grading (below target C1) in November 2024; four-year improvement plan required
findings.detail: Regulator of Social Housing inspection found gaps in tenant engagement, transparency, and service scrutiny reporting. Council has committed to improvement plan with next inspection in four years. The paper notes that 'Failure to meet the Social Housing Regulation Act requirements could result in enforcement action or fines.' The 2026/27 budget includes £30K additional growth specifically for tenant engagement to support compliance.
findings.matters: C2 rating indicates regulatory compliance weakness. Enforcement action or regulatory fines represent both financial and reputational risk, and affect operational credibility with lenders.
findings.figures: C2 rating from November 2024; next RSH inspection in four years; £30K added for tenant engagement improvement
findings.quote: The Council was inspected by the RSH in November 2024 and received a C2 consumer grading, indicating that while the Council meets many requirements of the Consumer Standards, improvements are needed in areas such as tenant engagement and transparency.

findings.headline: HRA requires £5.8M cumulative revenue savings by year 10 with explicit flagging of 'large financial risk' if missed
findings.detail: The 30-year plan assumes £5.8M in cost reductions or capital cuts by year 10. The council labels failure to hit this target as representing 'a large financial risk to the account.' The 2026/27 budget achieves £496K in savings (£285K staffing, £57K Business Change team, £45K ICT, £30K cleaning, £29K community development, £24K laundry closure, £22K customer services) but the quantum of future cuts and their deliverability remain unspecified.
findings.matters: A savings programme of this scale across 10 years carries execution risk, especially given the council's own assessment that missing it creates 'large financial risk.' This affects debt sustainability and capital investment capacity.
findings.figures: £5.8M cumulative savings required by year 10; £496K savings in 2026/27; £1M annual savings assumed from 2027/28 onwards
findings.quote: By year 10 of the model £5.8Million of total on-going savings will need to have been made from the revenue budget, or reduced capital expenditure and financing costs. This represents a significant fall in expenditure and not meeting this target represents a large financial risk to the account.

findings.headline: Building safety remediation costs materially underestimated; true scope and cost remain unquantified
findings.detail: After specialist consultancy review, the council identified that building safety remediation costs are 'likely to be much higher than previously estimated' but full costs remain unmodelled. The 2026/27 budget adds £513K for safety compliance (door inspections £178K, solar £83K, water systems £55K, fire remedial £235K, lift maintenance £56K), but the council explicitly commits to bringing a separate Cabinet report once cost modelling is complete, stating 'financial implications from these reviews are likely to be significant and have implications for the HRA Business Plan.'
findings.matters: The council has flagged material cost uncertainty on high-rise blocks representing significant infrastructure liability. Lenders need the true scope of remediation obligations and realistic costs before assessing creditworthiness.
findings.figures: £513K building safety growth in 2026/27; 95% of 11m+ housing stock requires remediation; costs described as 'likely to be much higher than previously estimated' but unquantified
findings.quote: The outcome of this review suggests that costs are likely to be much higher than previously estimated to remediate the blocks and to ensure compliance with relevant building safety legislation

findings.headline: Largest ICT budget item offers no Year 1 or Year 2 savings, dependent on pilot success
findings.detail: The £1,628,850 ICT budget contains conditional savings of £40k in 2028/29 'depending on the outcome of a proof of the concepts over the next nine months'. Shows £0 savings for both Year 1 and Year 2.
findings.matters: The council's largest service budget provides no certain near-term savings and relies entirely on speculative pilot outcomes, introducing uncertainty into core operations.
findings.figures: £1,628,850 baseline; £0 Year 1; £0 Year 2; £40k conditional 2028/29
findings.quote: Depending on the outcome of a proof of the concepts over the next nine months, replacing the virtual desktop solution with M365 will result in further savings of £40k in 2028/29.

findings.headline: Development waste charging income won't arrive until 2027/28, creating Year 1 gap
findings.detail: The council seeks 'approval at this stage to enable officers to begin issuing charging packs to external developers from this financial year (2025/26)', but explicitly states 'the projected additional income from bin deliveries will not materialise until 2027/28 onwards'. Year 1 savings are £0.
findings.matters: This creates a timing gap between implementation and revenue, potentially leaving a budget shortfall in Year 1 when the council needs savings now.
findings.quote: Although the projected additional income from bin deliveries will not materialise until 2027/28 onwards, approval is sought at this stage to enable officers to begin issuing charging packs to external developers from this financial year (2025/26)

findings.headline: Key planning fee increases lack calculated income figures despite approval
findings.detail: Fast Track planning applications (£2,910) and pre-application fee uplifts (£8,000) together represent £10,910 in proposed Year 1 savings, but are noted as 'Approved in October fees and Charges report but income not yet calculated'. The council is proposing these as budget savings despite not having determined the actual income.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that proposed savings will materialize; savings based on incomplete quantification represent material budget delivery risk.
findings.figures: £2,910 FastTrack; £8,000 pre-application uplift; £10,910 combined Year 1
findings.quote: Approved in October fees and Charges report but income not yet calculated

findings.headline: Decarbonisation funding gap of £110–128M means Council cannot afford net zero 2050 commitment without external funding
findings.detail: The Council is committed to achieving net zero by 2050, but full decarbonisation is not included in the 30-year business plan because the estimated additional cost of £110–128M is unaffordable without significant external funding. Only EPC C compliance by 2030 (cost to be absorbed) is funded within current plans. This represents a structural gap between the Council's strategic commitment and its financial capacity.
findings.matters: A strategic commitment that cannot be funded within the HRA's envelope creates reputational and financial risk. If external funding does not materialise or if regulatory requirements tighten on energy standards, the Council will face either unplanned capital spending or failure to deliver net zero targets.
findings.figures: £110–128M cost estimate for net zero by 2050; EPC C compliance by 2030 is funded; net zero not included in 30-year plan
findings.quote: full decarbonisation to achieve net zero by 2050 is not included in the current plan due to the estimated additional cost of £110m –£128m, which is unaffordable without significant external funding. The Housing Asset Management Service will continue to review its approach and seek grant funding opportunities to support delivery of energy efficiency improvements, contributing to the Council's Climate Change Strategy and Action Plan.

findings.headline: Awaab's Law implementation costs £80K in 2026/27 with expansion to further hazards over next two years
findings.detail: Implementation of Awaab's Law from October 2025 requires additional staffing of £80K in 2026/27. The law is also being expanded to other Housing Health and Safety Rating System (HHSRS) hazards over the next two years, suggesting further staffing resources will be needed beyond 2026/27 to ensure legal and regulatory compliance.
findings.matters: New legal requirements are creating permanent baseline cost pressures in the HRA budget, and the Council acknowledges that full implementation will likely require additional spending in future years beyond current forecasts.
findings.figures: £80K staffing cost for 2026/27; expansion over next two years; no forward-dated cost estimates given
findings.quote: An additional business support role has been funded from within existing budgets in 2025/26. However, with the implementation of Awaab's Law from October 2025 and expanded to the other "Housing Health and Safety Rating System" (HHSRS) potential hazards over the next two years, it is likely that staffing resources will need to increase to ensure legal and regulatory compliance.

findings.headline: Medium-term savings requirement of £5.8M by year 10 described as significant risk if not achieved
findings.detail: The HRA Business Plan requires £5.8M of total ongoing savings by year 10 of the 30-year plan, representing a significant fall in expenditure. The Council acknowledges that not meeting this target represents a large financial risk to the ring-fenced account. Current savings proposals for 2026/27 total only £496K (£705K after pension review benefit).
findings.matters: A savings requirement of this scale, explicitly flagged as high-risk by the Council itself, indicates the medium-term budget plan depends critically on delivery of service reductions or efficiency gains whose feasibility is uncertain. Failure to achieve these savings would force either rent increases above CPI+1%, capital spending cuts, or balance sheet drawdown.
findings.figures: £5.8M ongoing savings needed by year 10; £496K savings in 2026/27 identified; £1.7M required in 2027/28; £5.8M total by year 10
findings.quote: By year 10 of the model £5.8Million of total on-going savings will need to have been made from the revenue budget, or reduced capital expenditure and financing costs. This represents a significant fall in expenditure and not meeting this target represents a large financial risk to the account.

findings.headline: Rent convergence policy will create £209K income loss and £891K medium-term savings gap if Government decides not to approve it
findings.detail: The budget assumes rent convergence with a £1-per-week cap will be approved by January 2026, generating £209K additional income in 2026/27. However, the Government announcement has been delayed. If the policy is not implemented, the Council loses that income and faces £210K additional savings pressure in 2026/27 and £681K in 2027/28, with no identified solutions.
findings.matters: A material income assumption remains unconfirmed one month before the budget is finalised, creating uncertainty in the HRA's financial position and forcing the Council to carry savings risk into 2027/28 when the medium-term plan is already under strain.
findings.figures: £209K income impact if convergence not approved; £210K savings pressure in 2026/27; £681K in 2027/28
findings.quote: Although the Government have not confirmed whether they will include rent convergence in the final rent standard for April 2026, the draft budget proposal assumes that this will proceed with a maximum limit of £1 per week for this increase. If the Government's final decision is made in time, the final HRA Budget proposal will be amended to reflect this which could reduce rental income by £209K if they decide not to implement rent convergence.

findings.headline: Regulatory C2 consumer grading requires improvement plan over four years
findings.detail: The Regulator of Social Housing inspected the Council in November 2024 and gave a C2 consumer grading, indicating gaps in tenant engagement, transparency, and remedial action reporting. The Council has committed to an improvement plan and aims to achieve a C1 rating at the next inspection in four years. Additional funding of £30K in 2026/27 is allocated for tenant engagement activities to support regulatory compliance.
findings.matters: A lower regulatory grade indicates governance and service quality weaknesses, creating enforcement risk and signalling to lenders that management controls over service delivery need improvement.
findings.figures: C2 consumer grading (November 2024); £30K growth for tenant engagement; four-year improvement timeline to C1
findings.quote: The Council was inspected by the RSH in November 2024 and received a C2 consumer grading, indicating that while the Council meets many requirements of the Consumer Standards, improvements are needed in areas such as tenant engagement and transparency. The inspection confirmed strong compliance with health and safety obligations and effective repairs services, but highlighted gaps in reporting remedial actions and involving tenants in service scrutiny.

findings.headline: £1.06m MRP overpayment from regeneration assets now being reclaimed to offset future revenue charges
findings.detail: Historic voluntary MRP payments of £1,057,660.39 on regeneration assets have been identified as overpayment following review of asset lives in 2019/20. This overpayment is being reclaimed by reducing MRP charges in 2025/26 and later years, meaning no MRP will be charged on regeneration assets until 2025/26.
findings.matters: The overpayment reclamation materially affects the revenue budget for 2025/26 and represents a significant one-off benefit; the finance director needs to understand this is temporary relief, not a structural improvement.
findings.quote: The overpayment of £1,057,660.39 results in no MRP needing to be charged to the accounts for the regeneration assets until 2025/26, when a partial charge will be required, utilising the remainder of the overpayment balance.

findings.headline: Capital programme unfunded since 2013-14, financed from investment balances rather than external borrowing
findings.detail: The council has not had a fully funded capital programme in 12 years and has been financing capital expenditure using investment balances rather than taking external borrowing in full. This reliance on reserves to fund capital is not sustainable indefinitely and affects the council's balance sheet and future financial flexibility.
findings.matters: Lenders assessing the council's financial sustainability would need to understand whether this pattern continues and when external borrowing may become necessary, as it indicates the capital programme strategy is not self-supporting.
findings.figures: Since 2013/14
findings.quote: From 2013/14, the council has not had a fully funded capital programme, and although there has not been a need to borrow in full externally, due to the use of investment balances, it is necessary to make adequate provision for the repayment of debt

findings.paper_title: 8 Cabinet Report - HRA Business Plan 2026_27 to 2056_27 - FINAL
findings.headline: Housing stock is predominantly post-war (84% built 1950–1979) with ongoing decency and energy efficiency compliance costs
findings.detail: 84% of the 7,971-home stock was built between 1950–1979. Currently 1.5% of homes are below Decent Homes Standard, with a target of 100% compliance by 2026/27 and EPC rating C by 2030. This aging stock profile creates sustained investment and compliance pressure that could exceed budget if regulatory standards tighten.
findings.matters: Aging stock with high maintenance and energy retrofitting requirements creates ongoing capital pressure and regulatory compliance risk that can quickly escalate costs.
findings.figures: 84% of stock built 1950–1979, 1.5% currently non-decent, 100% decency target by 2026/27, EPC-C target by 2030
findings.quote: The Council's stock is predominantly post-war housing with 84% built between 1950–1979. The programme of stock condition surveys covers 96.9% of homes, with the level of non-decency currently at 1.5%, but the programme will ensure that all homes can meet the Decent Homes Standard in 2026/27

findings.paper_title: 8 Cabinet Report - HRA Business Plan 2026_27 to 2056_27 - FINAL
findings.headline: Minimum HRA reserves increased from £6M to £10M due to identified risks
findings.detail: The council has increased the minimum balance requirement for the HRA from £6M to £10M to manage risks including rent policy changes, interest rate volatility, regulatory compliance costs, and climate obligations. This increase signals heightened concern about financial resilience and may constrain spending flexibility.
findings.matters: Rising reserve requirements indicate the council expects greater volatility or risk; higher minimums reduce the buffer available for unexpected pressures.
findings.figures: Minimum reserves raised from £6M to £10M
findings.quote: the financial model has increased the minimum balance requirement for the HRA from £6Million to £10Million. This enhanced reserve position will provide the Council with greater flexibility to adjust operations and spending plans, allowing it to respond to emerging challenges

findings.paper_title: 8 Cabinet Report - HRA Business Plan 2026_27 to 2056_27 - FINAL
findings.headline: Capital investment programme of £745M over 30 years, with £148M required in first five years
findings.detail: Stock maintenance requires £148M in the first five years and £745M over the full plan. An additional £457M is allocated for new housing development. These commitments lock the council into sustained borrowing and create multi-year revenue pressure from financing costs that must be funded from rental income.
findings.matters: Large capital commitments create structural revenue pressure and constrain financial flexibility; any shortfall in rent income or subsidy affects the council's ability to deliver the programme.
findings.figures: £148M first 5 years, £745M over 30 years for stock investment; £457M for new housing development
findings.quote: A total of £148Million is programmed for stock investment in the first five years of the plan, and £745Million over 30 years. Investment priorities include building safety and compliance, Decent Homes and energy efficiency.

findings.paper_title: 8 Cabinet Report - HRA Business Plan 2026_27 to 2056_27 - FINAL
findings.headline: High revenue pressures affecting the first half of the 30-year plan period
findings.detail: The plan explicitly acknowledges 'high levels of revenue pressure in the first half of the Plan' driven by inflation, capital financing costs, and rent policy constraints. While conditions are forecast to ease in later years, the council faces near-term financial stress requiring careful management of spending and reserves.
findings.matters: Short-term revenue pressures increase risk of reserve depletion or forced service reductions within the medium-term financial strategy period.
findings.figures: First half of 30-year plan period
findings.quote: Overall, the financial model shows that there are high levels of revenue pressure in the first half of the Plan.

findings.paper_title: 8 Cabinet Report - HRA Business Plan 2026_27 to 2056_27 - FINAL
findings.headline: Medium-term savings requirement of £5.8M per annum needed by 2035/36 to balance the plan
findings.detail: The financial model explicitly requires £5.8M per annum in savings by 2035/36 to remain balanced. The council identifies this as particularly acute in the medium term. Failure to deliver these savings would leave the HRA in deficit and force additional borrowing, service reductions, or rent increases above policy.
findings.matters: Large unspecified savings requirements are a red flag; if not fully developed and actionable, they indicate unresolved financial pressures.
findings.figures: £5.8M per annum savings needed by 2035/36
findings.quote: Large savings needed to balance Plan, especially in the medium term of £5.8m per annum by 20235/36

findings.paper_title: 8 Cabinet Report - HRA Business Plan 2026_27 to 2056_27 - FINAL
findings.headline: Peak HRA debt forecast at £354M with debt servicing costs reaching 32% of annual income
findings.detail: The financial model forecasts peak debt of £354M in year six, representing 5.18 times annual income. Debt servicing costs peak at 32% of income. The council has approved immediate prudential borrowing of £35.6M in 2026/27 plus £7M refinancing. While slightly lower than the previous plan's peak debt, this remains a significant obligation dependent on maintaining rental income.
findings.matters: Lenders assess debt-to-income ratios and debt servicing costs as core viability metrics; at 5.18x income, debt capacity is constrained and vulnerable to income shortfalls.
findings.figures: £354M peak debt (year 6), 5.18x income, debt servicing at 32% of income, £35.6M new borrowing 2026/27, £7M refinancing
findings.quote: peak debt is forecast at £354Million in year six, equivalent to 5.18 times annual income and this is slightly lower than the last Plan. Another indicator is total debt servicing costs in year as a percentage of income. This peaks at 32%

findings.headline: Stevenage is recovering £1,057,660 in previously overpaid Minimum Revenue Provision
findings.detail: The council revised asset lives in 2019/20, resulting in an overpayment of MRP in prior years. Under MHCLG guidance, this overpayment can be reclaimed. Regeneration assets will bear no MRP charge until 2025/26, when a final partial charge of £89,144.79 will be applied, utilising the remainder of the overpayment balance.
findings.matters: This reduces the council's future revenue spending by approximately £195k annually, improving financial flexibility and reducing the cost of debt servicing.
findings.figures: £1,057,660.39 total overpayment; £193,703.12 charged annually 2020/21-2024/25; £89,144.79 final charge 2025/26
findings.quote: The overpayment of £1,057,660.39 results in no MRP needing to be charged to the accounts for the regeneration assets until 2025/26, when a partial charge will be required, utilising the remainder of the overpayment balance.

findings.headline: Capital expenditure spent at only 50% of budget, with significant reprofiling into future years
findings.detail: The council budgeted £88.4m capital expenditure but spent only £44.4m, a £44m underspend. This triggered 'reprofiling of planned capital expenditure from 2024/25 into future years'. The General Fund was particularly weak (£13.3m actual v £33.6m budget, 40% of plan). This suggests delivery risk or changing project timelines.
findings.matters: Capital delivery is a key test of a council's project management and spending discipline. Large year-on-year reprofiling can signal weak project pipelines, procurement delays, or slippage in regeneration plans. For the HRA in particular, underspend means delayed housing delivery.
findings.figures: Total capital expenditure: £44.421m actual v £88.389m budget (50%); General Fund £13.347m v £33.558m (40%); HRA £31.074m v £54.831m (57%)
findings.quote: There was reprofiling of planned capital expenditure from 2024/25 into future years resulted in an overall reduction in the use of borrowing to finance capital expenditure.

findings.headline: Under-borrowing strategy is acknowledged as contingent on high cash balances and faces future strain
findings.detail: The council deliberately maintains an under-borrowed position, using £46m in investments to avoid external borrowing while rates are high. Officers confirm this strategy 'only remains financially viable while cash balances are high' and note the risk that falling capital receipts and grant funding could force borrowing at higher rates than budgeted.
findings.matters: The council is using a cash-depletion model rather than matching borrowing to capital spending. When reserves fall (which the capital programme will cause), the council will be forced to borrow at whatever rates prevail, not the lower rates it could lock in now.
findings.figures: £46.132m in investments at 31 March 2025; average investment return 4.95%; PWLB borrowing at 4.87–4.88%
findings.quote: This policy only remains financially viable while cash balances are high. Capital investment, not funded by capital receipts and grant funding reduce these balances if not supported by additional borrowing. The risk is that the Council may need to take borrowing at higher rates than budgeted which would increase revenue costs.

findings.headline: HRA interest rate risk flagged against 30-year business plan sustainability
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies a risk to the Housing Revenue Account's ability to fund its approved 30-year spending plans if interest rates remain elevated. The HRA carries £272.4m in capital financing requirement and is currently paying £8.3m annually in PWLB interest. While the council expects rates to fall, sustained high rates could force difficult spending decisions on the HRA business plan.
findings.matters: The HRA's 30-year funding plan is the backbone of the council's housing strategy. Interest rate stress on a £272m debt portfolio could force a choice between capital investment, rent levels, or service cuts.
findings.figures: HRA CFR £272.356m; HRA PWLB interest paid £8.3m; expectations rates fall from 4.87–4.88% (new borrowing rates in July 2024) to 3.75% by end March 2026
findings.quote: There is a risk to the HRA BP's ability to fund the approved 30-year spending plans if interest rates continue at the current high level, although currently it is anticipated that rates will reduce.

findings.headline: Pension scheme triennial review due 2026/27 could increase employer contributions beyond the £100K allowance assumed in the MTFS
findings.detail: The council has made a £100K estimated allowance for increased Hertfordshire pension scheme contributions following the 2026/27 triennial valuation. However, the paper flags this as unknown: 'the financial impact will not be known until later in the current year prior to the 2026/27 budget setting'. Pension revaluations can produce significant adverse swings, especially given the high PWLB rates affecting gilt yields (which affect pension liability valuations).
findings.matters: Pension contributions are not discretionary and represent a committed cost. If the triennial review is worse than the £100K assumption, the council must either find savings elsewhere or draw on reserves. Timing (due later in 2025) means the amount will be known before the December settlement, but creates another moving target.
findings.figures: £100K allowance for 2026/27 Hertfordshire pension contribution increase
findings.quote: The 2026/27 inflation projections include £100K additional costs for the Hertfordshire triennial pension review, this in only an estimated allowance at this stage and the financial impact will not be known until later in the current year prior to the 2026/27 budget setting.

findings.headline: Balancing the Budget savings target (£2.284M over 2026/27–2029/30) is achievable in 2026/27 but dependent on Fair Funding materialising; beyond 2027/28 becomes the new unitary council's problem
findings.detail: The original MTFS published in February 2025 set a savings target of £2.4M. Fair Funding improvements have reduced this to £2.284M. The council has identified £1.15M of savings for 2026/27 (business change £418K, commercial £237K, fees and charges £358K pending approval, efficiency £121K). However, the paper explicitly states: 'the financial position of the Council is projected to be greatly improved as a result of the Fair Funding projections' and that savings targets beyond 2027/28 will 'if the timetable is followed be the preserve of the new unitary Council'. This means the council is deferring medium-term savings pressure to the merged authority.
findings.matters: A council that meets its short-term savings target only because of a contingent government funding decision is not demonstrating sustainable savings delivery. If Fair Funding falls short, the 2027/28–2029/30 targets will fall to the incoming unitary with no track record of achievement.
findings.figures: 2026/27 identified savings £1.15M; 2026/27 target £1.134M (exceeded, but includes £358K fees and charges 'provisional and subject to approval'); 2027/28–2029/30 targets £1.484M, £1.884M, £2.284M respectively
findings.quote: However, the change in government funding as set out in section 4.8 considerably alters the need for significant savings as even on a prudent estimate that funding will increase a total of £3.067Million.

findings.headline: Council tax collection rate remains at 94.5%, below other Hertfordshire councils, despite improvement initiatives
findings.detail: Stevenage's council tax collection rate in 2024/25 was 94.5%, which is 'generally lower than in other Hertfordshire Councils'. The council has implemented initiatives (banded discount scheme, arrears review, automation) to improve, but the weakness persists. The taxbase budget assumption includes a 2% bad debt provision (increased from 1.75%), acknowledging the collection risk.
findings.matters: A persistently weak collection rate signals either deprivation/hardship in the population or collection process inefficiency. It is a revenue risk; if collection does not improve, income falls short of projections. The higher bad debt assumption consumes revenue that could otherwise fund services.
findings.figures: 2024/25 collection rate 94.5%; bad debt provision 2% of collectable tax (increased from 1.75%)
findings.quote: The tax collected in year continues to be challenging (94.5% in 2024/25) and generally lower than in other Hertfordshire Councils, however the Shared Revenues and Benefits service with East Hertfordshire District Council is to trying to improve this by: [initiatives listed]

findings.headline: New borrowing approved for major capital projects (Garage £2.6M, Oval redevelopment £303K/year borrowing cost by 2029/30) at current PWLB rates of 5.79%
findings.detail: The council has approved and is planning new prudential borrowing for three major schemes: Garage Improvement Programme (£2.6M total 2026/27–2028/29, already approved), Oval redevelopment (indicative borrowing costs £137K in 2027/28, £275K in 2028/29, £275K in 2029/30), and a new Leisure Centre (to be reported October 2025). PWLB 25-year rates are currently 5.79%, which is significantly higher than the council's investment yield (~3%). Each £1M borrowed costs an extra £12.9K/year in net borrowing cost vs. using reserves.
findings.matters: These borrowing commitments lock in debt service over 20+ years at elevated rates. A lender assesses whether the council has headroom to absorb these costs and whether the projects (especially Oval and Leisure Centre) are generating sufficient returns. The CFO notes that 'having available reserves in the General Fund would allow some limited capital investment' and would 'ensure borrowing head room' for the Leisure Centre.
findings.figures: Garage: £2.6M approved; Oval: £303K/year borrowing cost by 2029/30; PWLB 25-year rate: 5.79%; net cost of borrowing vs. investment: £12.9K per £1M borrowed
findings.quote: If the General Fund needs to externally borrow as cash balances reduce below that required for day to day running of the Council, then this will increase expenditure in the General Fund for example, based on an average investment rate lost of 4.5% versus a borrowing rate currently of 5.79% is an extra £12,900 per million externally borrowed.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation transition costs assumed at £150K/year but CFO notes this 'could be higher than assumed'
findings.detail: Stevenage is merging into a larger unitary authority, with a shadow authority from 2027/28 and full vesting 2028/29. The MTFS assumes £150K/year for transition costs (officer capacity and external advice). However, the CFO explicitly flags that 'costs going into LGR could be higher than assumed in the MTFS at £150K per year'. This is an identified risk with no quantified ceiling.
findings.matters: LGR is a structural change with one-off and ongoing costs that are difficult to forecast. A lender needs to know whether £150K covers genuine requirements or is optimistic. If actual costs are significantly higher, it would draw on reserves or reduce capacity for other priorities.
findings.figures: £150K per year 2026/27–2028/29; also flagged as 'higher transition costs into LGR requiring further General Fund contributions' in risks section
findings.quote: The costs going into LGR could be higher than assumed in the MTFS at £150K per year from 2026/27 (assumed in MTFS).

findings.headline: Queensway LLP (council's town centre retail/residential joint venture) is in a 'challenging retail environment' and requires additional £50K/year reserve contribution
findings.detail: The council set up Queensway LLP as a regeneration vehicle for retail and residential units in the town centre. The Cabinet paper flags that this asset 'faces a challenging retail environment' and the CFO recommends setting aside an additional £50K per year (on top of existing support) to ensure its 'financial resilience'. This is growth of a financial liability tied to an underperforming commercial asset, not a temporary pressure.
findings.matters: A council's commercial ventures can become persistent drains on the general fund. Acknowledging that support must grow (from prior years' contributions) signals that the original investment case may not be delivering and the asset requires ongoing subsidy.
findings.figures: £50K per year recommended for 2026/27–2028/29; Queensway reserve closing balance projected £701K (2026/27) increasing to track growing cumulative subsidy
findings.quote: The Council's retail and residential income strip Queensway LLP faces a challenging retail environment as set out in the part two report to this Cabinet and the CFO recommends an additional £50K per year is set aside in the Queensway earmarked reserve to support the company.

findings.headline: Business rates reset in 2026/27 will eliminate most of the council's £1.2M annual gains; tariff increase means Stevenage drops from £1.24M (2025/26) to £200K assumption
findings.detail: Stevenage has benefited from business rates retention, with gains fluctuating £317K–£1.88M over recent years. The Fair Funding reset includes a tariff increase that will reduce retained gains substantially. The council now assumes only £200K/year going forward, a structural reduction from historical £1.2M. This is not a temporary shortfall but a permanent shift in the funding structure; gains are unlikely to recover 'for a few years due to the reset'.
findings.matters: A council that has relied on variable business rates gains loses a revenue stream when the system resets. The £1M drop forces either further savings or reserves drawdown. Combined with Fair Funding uncertainty, this creates a dual revenue shock risk.
findings.figures: 2025/26 estimated gains £1.39M; MTFS forward assumption £200K/year; implied reduction £1.19M annually
findings.quote: Reallocating growth and resetting Business Rates Baselines in 2026/27 will expose authorities to a higher risk of falling below their Baseline Funding Level, particularly in the first year following a reset before any growth accumulates again.

findings.headline: Fair Funding 2.0 consultation result still uncertain; council modelled as £1.36–2.0M gainer but assuming £500K/year 'ceiling' to account for potential post-consultation changes
findings.detail: The government's Fair Funding reform consultation closed 15 August 2025 but final settlement won't be known until mid-December. Stevenage models significant gains due to high needs assessment and low council tax base. However, the CFO has conservatively assumed a £500K annual reduction from stated gains ('ceiling on gains after consultation') for all three years 2026/27–2028/29 to account for possible policy changes. This creates material uncertainty around projected surplus.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council's projected improvement is guaranteed or contingent on a government decision that could still shift. If Fair Funding delivers less than the lower estimate, the council would face significant savings pressure.
findings.figures: Modelled gain range £1.36M–£3.9M (2026/27–2028/29); prudent MTFS assumes only £2.041M–£3.945M; £500K annual 'ceiling on gains' allowance applied to all three years
findings.quote: The outcome of the consultation will not be known until circa October/November 2025 and the provisional funding settlement just before parliament rises on the 18 December 2025, therefore the CFO considers it prudent to revise down the numbers (as set out above) until clarification is given later in the year.

news_drafts.headline: Stevenage Audit Committee sees MRP policy revised, with no charge on 2026/27 borrowing until 2027/28
news_drafts.lead:
Stevenage Borough Council is amending its policy on minimum revenue provision, the amount a council must set aside from each year's budget to pay off past borrowing, much like a mortgage repayment. The changes go to full Council for approval alongside the treasury management mid-year review for 2026/27, which the Audit Committee considered. The mid-year review says the amendments "clarify and strengthen the Council's compliance with the revised framework relating to capital loans to third parties" and the treatment of capital receipts financing.

Under the revised 2026/27 policy, capital spending financed by borrowing in 2026/27 will not be subject to a charge until 2027/28. For capital loans to third parties granted on or after 7 May 2024, the charge must be at least any recognised credit loss for the year, and capital receipts from the loan in that year do not reduce it. The council has determined that no charge is required on borrowing for housing assets in the housing revenue account, the ring-fenced account for council housing paid for by rents. It cites its duty to charge depreciation and its Major Repairs Reserve as meaning prudent provision has been made.

The policy also covers regeneration assets. Historic charges were overpaid, by a cumulative £1,057,660.39, when asset lives were revised. That overpayment has been used up at £193,703.12 a year from 2020/21 to 2024/25, and £89,144.79 in 2025/26, when the policy says "a partial charge will be applied, utilising the remainder of the overpayment balance."

news_drafts.headline: Stevenage took one new £12m Public Works Loan Board loan in 2025-26, at 4.31% over five years
news_drafts.lead:
Stevenage Borough Council's only new loan in 2025-26 was £12m from the Public Works Loan Board (PWLB, the government's lending arm for councils), drawn on 26 January 2026 at 4.31% a year and due for repayment on 24 January 2031. Its annual treasury management review (how the council borrows and invests its cash) went to the council meeting on 21 October 2026.

The loan refinanced an existing loan within the housing revenue account (HRA), the separate account for the council's own housing stock, which is paid for by rents. The papers describe it as replacing internal borrowing, meaning use of the council's own cash instead of a loan. That temporary use of cash became fixed-rate borrowing from the PWLB. The council also repaid £0.5m of existing PWLB debt during the year. The minutes record that the loan was taken "in accordance with the HRA 40-year Business Plan".

Total borrowing (external debt) stood at £266.057m on 31 March 2026, of which £259.487m was owed to the PWLB. The minutes put about £200m of the total down to HRA borrowing dating from the 2012 housing stock transfer. They record that the council operated within all its approved prudential indicators (the limits and measures every council must publish to show its borrowing is affordable) and stayed within its authorised limit, the maximum total debt it has told itself it will not exceed.

news_drafts.headline: Stevenage's accounts unverified for four years; auditors charge £258,000 to rebuild assurance
news_drafts.lead: Stevenage Council has received disclaimed audit opinions (where auditors could not confirm the accounts were true and fair) for four consecutive financial years from 2021/22 to 2024/25. This leaves its accounts unverified and opening balances carrying material uncertainty. The external auditor reports that significant transactions and management judgements from these years may not have been subject to audit at all. To rebuild assurance, auditors are charging an additional £258,471 in the current year, on top of standard audit fees of £226,032. The council does not expect a clean audit opinion until 2027/28. Auditors have flagged that success depends on the council's finance function being sufficiently resourced, and have identified specific risk factors around Queensway LLP transactions requiring investigation across all four years.
